title: EZEKIEL 23 CONTAINS SOME OF THE MOST GRAPHIC SEXUAL METAPHORS IN THE BIBLE—WHY?
paragraphs: EZEKIEL 23 CONTAINS SOME OF THE MOST GRAPHIC SEXUAL METAPHORS IN THE BIBLE—WHY?
The Chapter Most People Want to Skip May Be the Chapter That Exposes What We Have Been Hiding From God
There are passages in the Bible people underline.
There are passages they frame.
There are passages they quote when life is falling apart.
And then there is Ezekiel 23.
A chapter so disturbing that many Christians read a few verses, feel uncomfortable, close the Bible, and quietly move somewhere safer.
But maybe that discomfort is part of the point.
Because Ezekiel 23 was never written to entertain sexual curiosity.
It was written to destroy spiritual denial.
And if you can stay with this chapter long enough—without sanitizing it, sensationalizing it, or pretending its words are not there—you may discover something terrifying about sin...
and something breathtaking about the God who refuses to leave His people trapped inside it.
Ezekiel does not whisper.
He does not soften the imagery.
He gives us two symbolic sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, and then immediately tells us who they represent:
Samaria and Jerusalem.
This is crucial.
The chapter is not primarily a story about two literal sexually promiscuous women.
God identifies the women with covenant communities.
“Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 23:4).
In Hebrew, the verse reads in part:
“שֹׁמְרוֹן אָהֳלָה וִירוּשָׁלִַם אָהֳלִיבָה”
Shomron Oholah, vi-Yerushalayim Oholivah.
Samaria is Oholah.
Jerusalem is Oholibah.

Even their names carry theological weight. Oholah is commonly understood in connection with “her tent,” while Oholibah carries the sense “my tent is in her.” The imagery points toward worship and sanctuary: Samaria had established its own rival religious system, while Jerusalem possessed the LORD’s sanctuary.
And suddenly the scandal becomes deeper.
This is not merely about sexual behavior.
It is about worship.
It is about covenant betrayal.
It is about people who belonged to God reaching toward idols, nations, political powers, military strength, and foreign alliances as though those things could give them what only God could give.
Ezekiel takes invisible apostasy...
and gives it a body.
That is why the imagery becomes so uncomfortable.
Because idolatry rarely feels as disgusting to us as it should.
We hear the word “idol” and imagine a little statue sitting on an ancient shelf.
God saw something far more intimate.
Betrayal.
His people had been rescued, claimed, loved, sustained, warned, and called to belong to Him—and yet their hearts repeatedly ran toward other gods and other powers.
So Ezekiel refuses to let apostasy remain an abstract theological word.
He makes betrayal feel like betrayal.
He makes unfaithfulness look like unfaithfulness.
He makes spiritual adultery impossible to perfume.
And then comes the verse almost everyone remembers once they encounter this chapter.
Ezekiel 23:20.
The Hebrew itself is deliberately graphic:
“אֲשֶׁר בְּשַׂר־חֲמוֹרִים בְּשָׂרָם וְזִרְמַת סוּסִים זִרְמָתָם”

The wording compares the sexual anatomy of the desired lovers to donkeys and their emission to stallions. That is not an exaggeration invented by a provocative modern translation. The underlying Hebrew itself contains the animal comparison and the explicit reference.
Why would Scripture contain something like that?
Because God is not trying to arouse the reader.
He is exposing degradation.
The language is grotesque because the idolatry being portrayed is grotesque.
What Jerusalem regarded with fascination, Ezekiel portrays in humiliating, animalistic terms.
What looked impressive from a distance was spiritually degrading up close.
What appeared powerful...
was enslaving them.
And there is something painfully modern about that.
Sin still advertises itself better than it delivers.
It photographs beautifully.
It whispers, “You deserve this.”
It says, “Nobody needs to know.”
It says, “Just once.”
It says, “You can stop whenever you want.”
It says, “God is withholding something from you.”
And somehow what once disgusted you can eventually become what you defend.
What you once resisted can become what you secretly revisit.
What you once confessed with tears can become something you rename so you no longer have to call it sin.
That is why Ezekiel 23 can feel so invasive.
The chapter does not merely ask, “What have you done?”
It asks something more frightening:
What has your heart learned to desire instead of God?
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you still go to church.
Maybe you know when to raise your hands.
Maybe your Bible app still sends you a verse every morning.
Maybe people call you strong in the faith.
And maybe there is still a locked room inside your heart where Jesus is welcome to stand outside...
but not enter.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Pornography you keep promising to quit.
Bitterness you have baptized as discernment.
Money that stopped being a tool and became your security.
Attention you need so badly that silence feels like death.
A secret conversation.
A hidden addiction.
A hunger for admiration.
A career you would compromise almost anything to protect.
A political identity that stirs more passion in you than the kingdom of Christ.
A religious image you carefully maintain because admitting weakness feels more frightening than remaining enslaved.
An idol does not need a carved face.
Sometimes an idol is simply anything we ask to give us what we should ultimately seek in God.
Security.
Identity.
Worth.
Deliverance.
Meaning.
Power.
Love.
And this is where Ezekiel 23 becomes almost unbearable.
Because Jerusalem had evidence.
She had watched Samaria fall.
She knew where the road led.
And she followed it anyway.
That is one of the darkest mysteries of sin.
Sometimes we know.
We know the relationship is destroying us.
We know the habit is hollowing us out.
We know the secret is poisoning our prayer life.
We know that every time we return to it, something inside us becomes quieter.
We have watched other people wreck themselves on the same rocks.
And still...
we swim toward them.
Ezekiel describes Oholibah remembering Egypt and returning in desire to the patterns associated with her earlier unfaithfulness.
Memory became temptation.
The past became romanticized.
Bondage started looking beautiful again.
Have you ever noticed how sin edits your memories?
It shows you the pleasure...
and deletes the aftermath.
It reminds you of the intoxication...
and hides the shame.
It shows you Egypt’s food...
and somehow makes you forget Egypt’s chains.

That is why one of the most haunting lines in this chapter comes in Ezekiel 23:27, where God declares that He will put an end to this corruption so that His people will no longer look longingly toward Egypt or remember it in the same way.
The Hebrew contains the words:
“וְהִשְׁבַּתִּי זִמָּתֵךְ מִמֵּךְ”
Vehishbatti zimmatekh mimekh...
“I will cause your depravity/lewdness to cease from you...”
Do not rush past that.
God is not indifferent to what destroys His people.
His holiness is not passive.

His judgment in Ezekiel 23 is severe, and we should not dilute that severity. The chapter ends not with God shrugging at idolatry, but with accountability: they will bear the consequences of their idolatry and “know that I am the Lord GOD” (Ezekiel 23:49).
Grace never means God discovers that sin was harmless after all.
The Bible’s grace is infinitely more costly than that.
Sin is so serious that forgiveness does not come through God pretending evil does not matter.
And this is where we must read Ezekiel carefully.

Ezekiel 23 itself is overwhelmingly a chapter of accusation and judgment. We should not force the cross into every metaphor as though Ezekiel’s original audience could see every detail we see after Christ.
But Ezekiel’s book does not end in chapter 23.
Keep reading.
The God who exposes corruption will later speak of cleansing.
“I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean” (Ezekiel 36:25).
The God confronting hardened hearts will promise:
“I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And then:
“I will put my Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:27).
That movement matters.
Exposure.
Judgment.
Cleansing.
A new heart.
A new spirit.
Restoration.
And when Christians reach the New Testament, the Gospel announces how staggering the cost of reconciliation truly is.
Jesus does not arrive telling sinners to clean themselves sufficiently so He can finally love them.
Christ comes for sinners.
He calls them to repent and believe.
He touches the unclean.
He receives the broken.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He forgives the repentant.
And ultimately...
He goes to the cross.
Paul writes:
Not when we finally became impressive.
Not when the browser history became clean enough.
Not when the addiction disappeared.
Not when the marriage was repaired.
Not when every theological question was answered.
Not when we became worthy.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
Jesus begins His public proclamation with the call to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15).
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is not self-hatred.
Repentance is not performing enough sadness to convince God you deserve another chance.
The New Testament word is μετάνοια—metanoia—a turning of mind and life toward God, a change of direction that bears fruit.
Grace does not say, “Stay exactly where your chains have you.”
Grace says, “Come to Christ.”
And Christ does not merely offer better chains.
He offers Himself.
Maybe that is why this chapter bothers us so much.
Ezekiel 23 strips away the flattering names we give our idols.
It asks what happens when the thing you call “freedom” is actually mastering you.
When “I deserve to be happy” becomes permission to disobey God.
When “this is just how I am” becomes a fortress against repentance.
When “nobody is getting hurt” ignores what sin is doing to your soul.
When “God understands” quietly becomes “God will never confront me.”
He does understand.
Far more deeply than we do.
And precisely because He is holy and loving, He confronts what destroys.
Somebody reading this has been asking God for freedom while protecting the very thing from which you want freedom.
You pray about it.
Then reopen it.
You cry about it.
Then contact them again.
You delete it.
Then reinstall it.
You confess enough to reduce the guilt...
but not enough to kill the secrecy.
And perhaps your deepest fear is not that God knows.
Your deepest fear is that if you finally surrender, He will take away the thing you cannot imagine living without.
But what if the thing you cannot imagine living without...
is the thing keeping you from learning how to truly live?
The Gospel does not offer cosmetic improvement.
Jesus did not die so we could decorate our prison cells with Bible verses.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
So stop negotiating with the idol.
Stop giving respectable names to what God has already exposed.
Stop waiting until you “feel spiritual enough” to come home.
Bring Him the ugly thing.
Bring Him the history.
Bring Him the relapse.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the secret messages.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the appetite for approval.
Bring Him the shame you are terrified somebody will discover.
Bring Him the version of you that you have spent years making sure nobody sees.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because it matters so much that Christ went to the cross.
The scandal of Christianity is not that God calls evil good.
He never does.
The scandal is that the Holy One makes a way for guilty people to be forgiven without calling their guilt innocence.
At the cross, grace is not cheap.
It is blood-bought.
Peter says Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
Bring us to God.
That is the destination.
Not merely a better mood.
Not merely a cleaner reputation.
Not merely becoming religious.
God.
And maybe you have spent years thinking your story is too dirty for that.
Read Ezekiel 23 again.
Look at how ugly covenant betrayal is allowed to appear on the page.
Scripture does not need your life to be sanitized before it can tell the truth about you.
And then look at Jesus.
The woman publicly known as sinful could weep at His feet.
The tax collector could come down from the tree.
The thief dying beside Him could cry for mercy.
Peter could deny Him and later be restored.
Saul could persecute the church and become a servant of the Gospel.
The cross stands in the middle of human wreckage and announces that your sin is worse than your excuses admit...
and Christ’s mercy is greater than your shame wants you to believe.
That is the emotional violence of grace.
It destroys boasting and despair at the same time.
You cannot say, “I am good enough.”
The cross says you needed a Savior.
But you also cannot say, “I am too far gone.”
The cross says, “Look at the Savior.”
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by editing sin out of your history.
Not by calling darkness light.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking sinners who deserved judgment, washing them, forgiving them, reconciling them to God, and beginning the transforming work of making them new.
That is why your testimony does not have to be:
“Look how perfect I became.”
It can be:
“Look how merciful Christ has been.”
And if something in this article exposed a room inside you that you have kept locked for too long, do not perform spirituality right now.
Be honest.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It does not.
But sometimes bringing what has lived in darkness into honest confession is the first visible sign that you are finished pretending.
And if you see someone else comment that they are struggling, do not crush them.
Pray for them.
Encourage them toward Christ.
Remind them that repentance is not the end of hope.
It is the collapse of the lie that we can save ourselves.
There may be a night when Egypt starts looking beautiful again.
There may be a night when the old addiction starts rewriting your memories.
There may be a night when the person God delivered you from suddenly seems irresistible again.
Come back and remember:
Chains can become nostalgic when you forget what captivity cost you.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because an algorithm can measure faithfulness. It cannot.

If you want to glorify God through Gospel-centered digital ministry, one practical way you can help is by supporting and sharing work that keeps pointing people back to Scripture and Jesus Christ. But it can materially support the continued creation and distribution of biblical content so that more people encounter the Gospel.
Not to prove you love Jesus.
Follow because discipleship requires more than occasional inspiration.
And comment because somebody reading beneath you may need to know they are not the only person fighting to come back to Christ.
Then pray.
Actually pray.
Turn toward Christ.
Confess what needs confessing.
Seek trustworthy pastoral help and Christian accountability where you need it.
Make restitution where repentance requires it.
Cut off access where temptation repeatedly enters.
And do not confuse reading an emotional article with surrendering your life to Jesus.
The article cannot save you.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A comment cannot save you.
A church membership cannot save you.
Your tears cannot save you.
Your promises to “do better this time” cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
And perhaps that is ultimately why Ezekiel 23 is still in our Bible.
Because before grace feels amazing, sometimes we need to remember what grace is rescuing us from.
The chapter is ugly because sin is ugly.
The judgment is terrifying because holiness is real.
And the Gospel is breathtaking because the God against whom we have sinned has made reconciliation possible through His Son.
So when the old Egypt calls your name again...
remember the chains.
When your idol promises life again...
remember what it took from you.
When shame whispers that you are too filthy to return...
look to Christ.
When pride whispers that you do not need to return...
look to the cross.
And when you finally bring the hidden thing into the light, you may discover that Jesus was never waiting for a prettier version of your confession.
He was calling you to come.
The thing you are most afraid to surrender may be standing between you and the freedom you keep asking Jesus to give you.
